content.title: Permutations, Combinations, and the Multiplication Counting Principle
content.overview: This lesson covers the fundamental techniques for counting the number of ways to select or arrange items from a set. It focuses on the Multiplication Counting Principle, Permutations (where order matters), and Combinations (where order does not matter).
learning_objectives: Apply the Multiplication Counting Principle to sequential independent choices.
Distinguish between scenarios where order matters (permutations) and where it does not (combinations).
Calculate the number of permutations for a subset of items.
Calculate the number of combinations for a subset of items.

sections.title: The Multiplication Counting Principle
sections.content: The Multiplication Counting Principle is the foundation of all counting problems. If a task consists of a sequence of steps, where the first step can be done in 'n' ways, the second in 'm' ways, and so on, the total number of ways to complete the task is the product (n × m × ...). This applies when choices are independent. If items cannot be reused (no replacement), the number of available options decreases by one at each subsequent step.

sections.title: Permutations: When Order Matters
sections.content: A permutation is an arrangement of items in a specific order. Use permutations when the problem mentions distinct positions, such as 'first, second, and third place,' 'left-to-right on a shelf,' or specific roles like 'President and Vice President.' The formula for the number of ways to arrange 'k' items from a set of 'n' items is P(n, k) = n! / (n - k)!. Practically, this is calculated by multiplying 'k' descending integers starting from 'n'.

sections.title: Combinations: When Order Does Not Matter
sections.content:
A combination is a selection of items where the arrangement or order is irrelevant. Use combinations when you are simply choosing a group, committee, or set where members are equal. The formula for choosing 'k' items from 'n' is C(n, k) = n! / [k!(n - k)!]. Notice that C(n, k) is always smaller than P(n, k) because we divide by k! to 'remove' the duplicate arrangements of the same group.

![A flowchart to decide between Multiplication Principle, Permutations, and Combinations.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/1e562aab-51c2-4eda-be6e-d0c822778adc-1786506240670-298.webp)

worked_examples.question: A club with 10 members needs to choose a President, a Secretary, and a Treasurer. How many different ways can these roles be filled if no member can hold more than one office?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Determine if order matters. Since the roles (President, Secretary, Treasurer) are distinct, the order of selection matters. This is a permutation. Step 2: Identify n and k. n = 10 members, k = 3 roles. Step 3: Apply the Multiplication Counting Principle. There are 10 choices for President, 9 remaining choices for Secretary, and 8 remaining choices for Treasurer. Step 4: Multiply: 10 × 9 × 8 = 720. There are 720 ways.

worked_examples.question: A pizza shop offers 7 different toppings. How many different 3-topping pizzas can be made?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Determine if order matters. A pizza with pepperoni, mushrooms, and onions is the same as a pizza with onions, mushrooms, and pepperoni. Order does not matter. This is a combination. Step 2: Identify n and k. n = 7 toppings, k = 3 selections. Step 3: Calculate the permutation first: 7 × 6 × 5 = 210. Step 4: Divide by the factorial of the number of items selected (3!) to remove order: 210 / (3 × 2 × 1) = 210 / 6 = 35. There are 35 ways.

common_mistakes: Treating a combination problem as a permutation, resulting in a number that is too large.
Forgetting to reduce the number of available options in sequential steps when items cannot be repeated.
Dividing by the wrong factorial when calculating combinations.
exam_tips: Keywords for Permutations: arrange, line up, order, rank, distinct positions.
Keywords for Combinations: select, choose, group, committee, set.
If you are unsure, ask: 'Does changing the order of these items create a different outcome?' If yes, it's a permutation.
On the ACT, you can often solve permutation problems by drawing 'slots' for each choice and multiplying the number of options for each slot.
content.recap: To solve counting problems, first decide if order matters. If it does, multiply the number of options for each position (Permutation). If it does not, calculate the permutation and then divide by the factorial of the number of items selected (Combination).

knowledge_claims.content: The Multiplication Counting Principle states that the total number of outcomes for a sequence of independent steps is the product of the number of choices at each step.
In counting problems, order matters if the items are placed in distinct positions, such as specific job titles or ranked rankings.
In counting problems, order does not matter if the items are selected as a single group or set where the internal arrangement is irrelevant.
A permutation is a specific arrangement of a set of items where the order is significant.
A combination is a selection of items from a set where the order of selection is not significant.
To calculate P(n, k), multiply k consecutive descending integers starting from n.
To calculate C(n, k), divide the number of permutations P(n, k) by k! (k factorial).
For the same values of n and k (where k > 1), the number of combinations C(n, k) will always be less than the number of permutations P(n, k).
A common error is failing to decrease the number of options in the Multiplication Counting Principle when items cannot be reused (no replacement).
To verify if a problem requires a combination, check if swapping two selected items results in the exact same outcome.
The factorial of a number n (written as n!) is the product of all positive integers from n down to 1.
When arranging all n items in a set, the total number of permutations is n!.

videoLesson.title: Model Sequential Counting For Permutations
videoLesson.description: Recognize when order matters by checking for distinct positions or arrangements. List sequential choices, multiply options (reducing counts if no replacement), and divide by factorial only to remove order.
